brief.subject: Diesel drops 19 cents as spot rates climb; port strike risk grows
brief.headline: Diesel Falls to $5.937 While Spot Rates Rise; LA-Long Beach Strike Risk Builds
brief.dek: Fuel relief, firmer spot pricing, fresh fraud and theft warnings, and labor trouble brewing at the nation's busiest container port.
brief.lede: Diesel fell 19.0 cents to $5.937 a gallon this week, while spot rates moved higher. That combination is widening margins for carriers hauling on the spot market.

sections.heading: Diesel Slides Below $6
bullets: $5.937 per gallon is the national diesel average for the week of 2026-11-16, lowering per-mile fuel cost.
Down 19.0 cents (3.1%) from the prior week, the biggest relief at the pump in recent weeks.
Down 33.9 cents over four weeks, which also shrinks fuel surcharge revenue on contract freight.
Forecasts now point to a 2026 crude surplus, though geopolitical tensions keep risk alive.

sections.heading: Spot Rates Climb Against Fuel
bullets: Dry van spot rates hit a new high even as fuel prices fell, an unusual split that favors spot haulers.
Despite strong headline numbers, many carriers still find rates disappointing heading into routing-guide season.
One analyst sees tight capacity driving a longer, steadier rate cycle into 2027, though that is a forecast.

sections.heading: Fraud and Theft Stay Hot
bullets: The ATA is pushing FMCSA to tighten ELD certification so the devices are harder to exploit in freight fraud.
Organized crews are stealing cargo from slow-moving trains in California, a sign theft rings keep adapting.
$1.5 million in drugs was intercepted after ABF Freight workers flagged a shipment, and a fraudulent-ID pickup led to four guilty pleas.
Verify every pickup's identity and paperwork, because bad actors are targeting all modes.

sections.heading: LA-Long Beach Labor Trouble
bullets: Employers say contract talks with an ILWU local have stalled, raising strike risk at the busiest U.S. container port.
A disruption could strand drayage capacity and scramble outbound loads from Southern California.
5 million container units moved through the Port of LA in five months, its best stretch in 118 years.
